extracted.intended_audience: readers and contributors of Nature (scientists, educated general readers, authors of books and correspondence)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and expectations for writing and evaluating scientific book reviews, textbook revisions, monographs, methodological papers, models, and letters to the editor in a general scientific journal. Covers accuracy, audience, pedagogy, illustrations, experimental reporting, and editorial submission practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: State intended audience and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The book should be 'written for the many observers who use telescopes for study or pleasure and desire more information about their construction and properties' — i.e. clearly state its target readership and collect material accessible to the ordinary reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the scope and intended readership explicit; collect and present essential information so ordinary readers can access material otherwise scattered in specialist papers. Anti-pattern: a work that assumes specialist prior knowledge without signposting or explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical accuracy and proper sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid unverified or misleading historical statements (e.g. presenting Newton as a 'blunderer' without careful sourcing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify historical anecdotes and trace claims to original sources before repeating them. Antipatterns: repeating speculative suggestions as fact; failing to trace an assertion to its primary source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical correctness in descriptive passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical descriptions (e.g. optical arrangements, the measure of the field in Galilean glass, prism systems) must be correct and not copied verbatim if incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure technical descriptions are theoretically and practically accurate; when citing earlier accounts, prefer complete/theoretically correct descriptions (e.g. Herschel's) over incomplete ones. Antipattern: copying an incomplete or incorrect description that misleads readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate tone and polished composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Style and composition matter; inelegant or crude expressions ('credulous twaddle', 'pricked up its ears', 'blast of hot air') detract from the pleasure of perusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a tone suited to the audience and subject; avoid gratuitous colloquialisms or pejorative phrasing that undermines credibility. Scoring note: style can lower perceived quality even if technical content is sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textbook revision — eliminate all blunders
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviser must 'eliminate all possible blunders' (spelling, factual errors, misstatements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for typographical, spelling, and factual mistakes (examples given: misspelt place-names, outdated factual claims). Antipatterns: publishing a new edition that repeats obvious errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textbook revision — bring the work thoroughly up-to-date
rubrics_metrics.description: A revision must 'bring the work thoroughly up-to-date' (update facts, include recent methods and important recent examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include recent developments (e.g. new deepest boreholes, newer commonly adopted machinery, more important sinkings) and revise lists of commonly adopted equipment or methods. Failure to update undermines usefulness to students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textbook revision — remove ambiguity likely to puzzle students
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviser must 'see that there is no ambiguity likely to puzzle the student.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify concepts that students commonly confuse (example: distinguish clearly between work and power), reconcile differing formulas and explain discrepancies so students are not left with wrong impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and clarity of illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations must be more than mere sketches and should be well executed and informative (example: plan of a horizontal winding engine should show valves and valve-rods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide accurate, detailed diagrams proportionate to the text's pedagogic needs. Antipattern: crude or incomplete figures that mislead or omit essential components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise absolute accuracy over time-saving in serious research
rubrics_metrics.description: For crystallography and similar precise sciences, accuracy should be placed before time-saving: 'it is most sincerely to be hoped that serious crystallographic research is not to be so circumscribed, and that absolute accuracy will be placed before time-saving.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid adopting practices that trade reproducibility or absolute measurement accuracy for speed. Scoring note: methods optimized for quick cataloguing are unsuitable for work intended to establish precise measurements or foundational results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement and reporting practices (critique of time-saving proposals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author’s proposed practices — 'two, or at most three, crystals be measured', 'the indices be determined by a time-saving method', 'the mean observed angles be published without any citation of limits' — are presented but critiqued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting measurements, include sufficient sampling, state limits/uncertainties, and avoid publishing mean values without citation of measurement limits. Antipattern: reporting mean observed angles with no uncertainties or justification of sample size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain technical terms and write for beginners
rubrics_metrics.description: Introductory texts should be 'written in colloquial language' and 'careful to explain the technical terms' used freely by specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing beginners, avoid specialist jargon or define it clearly; use accessible analogies (example: 'water circuit analogy' for electrical circuits). Pedagogic note: early introduction of measurement concepts helps understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogic sequencing — introduce measurement concepts early
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce measurement of quantities (e.g. electrical energy) at an early stage for students to develop understanding (the author found early measurement effective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence material so that key measurable concepts are introduced early to ground theoretical ideas. Antipattern: postponing measurement/quantification to late chapters, leaving beginners with only abstract concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness and engagement with contemporary theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Monographs should cover relevant subject matter comprehensively (example: omission of polar climates is an oversight) and discuss recent competing theories (e.g. modern monsoon theories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include topics that current knowledge supports as sufficiently known; discuss and compare recent theories rather than omitting alternative or newer explanations. Scoring note: failure to discuss significant modern theories or leaving out known regions weakens the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful use of analogies and appropriate limits of comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing disparate domains (e.g. New Testament healing miracles and modern psychotherapy), be cautious: parallels may be 'not sufficiently exact to carry absolute conviction' and observation limits must be acknowledged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State limitations of historical observations and be cautious about analogies that overreach; acknowledge when source observations are unscientific or imprecise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough referencing and review of prior literature in correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters and scientific commentary should review and cite prior observations and publications (examples: citing Kent, Takamine and Yamada, Zeeman, King, Wing) when disputing or reinterpreting results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey prior literature, compare conditions and findings, and explain how new observations align or conflict with earlier work. Antipattern: claiming novelty while ignoring relevant precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify experimental conditions and consider reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental accounts must specify conditions (e.g. excitation method, vapour density, vacuum arc vs carbon arc) because different conditions produce different spectral structures or effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report apparatus, excitation conditions, concentrations/densities, and other parameters that can affect outcomes; discuss how results change with conditions and whether observations are reproducible under varied setups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model construction: mechanical plausibility, experimental demonstrability, and publish full descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical/physiological models (e.g. cochlea model) should surmount mechanical difficulties, be capable of experimental demonstration (respond to tuning-forks, show damping/spread of resonance), and be described fully in accessible publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish full descriptions and demonstration data in refereed outlets; ensure model reflects known mechanical/physiological constraints (e.g. continuity of basilar membrane), allows testable predictions, and can be refined. Scoring note: models that cannot be demonstrated or lack published methods are of limited utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial submission policy and author responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Editor states: 'The Editor does not hold himself responsible for opinions expressed by his correspondents. Neither can he undertake to return, or to correspond with the writers of, rejected manuscripts intended for this or any other part of NATURE. No notice is taken of anonymous communications.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit signed communications; do not expect returned manuscripts or individual correspondence about rejected submissions; understand that published letters carry the authors' opinions. Antipattern: sending anonymous communications or assuming editorial feedback/return of manuscripts.
